In PQK and QEL, concentration is primarily governed by entanglement and quantum dynamical expressivity, with reservoir depth emerging as a key factor in QEL architectures. We further study bandwidth scaling as a general mechanism for controlling encoding expressivity across all models. Our results indicate that bandwidth scaling effectively reduces concentration in moderate regimes by restricting the effective expressivity of the encoding, though this protective effect diminishes in highly expressive structural settings.

title: Classical simulability and hardware diagnostics for QAOA on geographic coverage benchmarks
summary: Quantum-optimization benchmarks can show reduced energy while concealing local loss of weighted covariance. We combine encoding checks with exact structural references to select informative circuit diagnostics for static geographic coverage instances. The executed 24-qubit surrogate has infeasible ground states, whereas a faithful 51-qubit slack encoding preserves its 13 support-graph components and remains exactly simulable blockwise. At the executed angles, the total ideal optimum probability is $5.47\times10^{-20}$, making optimum counts uninformative at the executed budget of $10^5$ shots. A product distribution with the measured bit marginals accounts for about $90\%$ of the observed energy reduction. In three fixed-circuit jobs, the global weighted-covariance ratio is approximately $0.50$, while a five-variable block has ratios between $0.12$ and $0.28$ and contributes only $3.7\%$ of the ideal global denominator. Simultaneous bands resolve its deficit relative to the global ratio under an exploratory conditional counting model. The exact block reference thus reveals a local discrepancy concealed by the aggregate, without identifying an error mechanism or establishing device stability. The procedure links benchmark structure to the resolution and limitations of its observables.

title: Actively stabilized Fabry-Pérot notch filters for correlated photons from cold two-level atoms
summary: We report two actively stabilized Fabry-Pérot cavities operated as reflection-mode notch filters for biphotons generated by spontaneous four-wave mixing in a cold two-level atomic ensemble. In this source, elastic scattering at the excitation frequency increases the single-detector count rates and the accidental-coincidence background, thereby limiting the observed nonclassical correlations. One cavity is placed in each photon-collection mode. An acousto-optic modulator frequency-dithers an auxiliary field, and synchronous demodulation of the transmitted power provides the locking discriminator. Light resonant with the auxiliary field is transmitted, whereas the detuned components are reflected toward the photon detectors. By tuning the auxiliary field to the same frequency as the excitation field, we filter these components and direct a larger portion of the quantum-correlated sidebands to the detection. The cavities have linewidths of approximately 2 MHz and remain locked for longer than a typical correlation acquisition. The measured Cauchy-Schwarz parameter exceeds unity in both configurations, with a higher central value with filtering ($\overline{R} = 4.15 \pm 0.93$) than without ($\overline{R} = 2.33 \pm 0.20$). This architecture provides actively stabilized rejection of a narrow spectral interval, simultaneously, for two fields detected in different directions. Filter performance could be further improved by adjusting the cavity linewidth to better match the spectral width of the central component and by reducing losses in the filters.

title: Communication advantages of a quantum switch of two pure-loss channels
summary: The quantum switch can enable communication through otherwise unusable channels, a phenomenon known as causal activation. We show that a switch of two identical pure-loss channels can achieve strictly greater energy-constrained classical and quantum capacities than their sequential use, even when two-way classical communication is available. Remarkably, the switch also activates quantum communication over a range of transmissivities for which the sequential channel has zero quantum capacity.

title: Block Search Conditioned on Features for Sequential Quantum Data Encoding
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure. Prepared for ESANN 2027. Code and reproduction scripts: https://github.com/CeciliaBotelho/ESANN-2026
summary: Sequential quantum data encoding is addressed through the joint selection of input features and encoding blocks within a fixed quantum register. At each step, a new feature, a block of operations, its placement, and its rotation weights are selected together from training data, extending the incremental construction of Q-FLAIR. With direct-loss selection (RAW), nine to twelve features were retained in four qubits across five new Bars and Stripes datasets. Under the same final calibration, mean changes relative to the calibrated Q-FLAIR reference were +5.53 percentage points in balanced accuracy, -15.83% in binary cross-entropy (BCE), and +7.79% in area under the ROC curve (AUC). The prespecified success criterion was met in four of five datasets and for the mean paired differences. These results were obtained by comparing complete procedures under a common cap of 32 operations.

title: Criterion and Construction Framework for Impure Quantum $(r,δ)$-LRCs from Optimal $(r,δ)$-LRCs
summary: This paper aims to uncover new phenomena and provide new tools for quantum \((r,δ)\)-LRCs derived from optimal \((r,δ)\)-LRCs. The initial motivation is to identify the main reason for the existence of impure cases in such quantum codes. Our main result reveals that whether \(d = r+1\) is the key factor governing the impurity of quantum \((r,δ)\)-LRCs. We prove that, when \(d \neq r+1\), impure quantum codes derived from optimal \((r,δ)\)-LRCs have bounded lengths. Conversely, when \(d = r+1\), we construct impure quantum \((r,δ)\)-LRCs with unbounded lengths. The central tool developed in this work is a criterion for identifying impure quantum codes derived from optimal \((r,δ)\)-LRCs. The main results include a criterion for impurity in quantum \((r,δ)\)-LRCs (Theorem 3.2), a construction framework for impure quantum \((r,δ)\)-LRCs (Theorem 4.4), and two families of impure quantum \((r,δ)\)-LRCs (Theorems 4.8 and 4.11).

title: Quantum control of an electrically levitated nanoparticle with a trapped ion
summary: Quantum control of levitated nanoparticles offers a route towards macroscopic quantum states. Here we propose a novel way to achieve it for a nanoparticle levitated electrically in a linear Paul trap together with a single ion, a system recently realized experimentally. By suitably engineering the trap's AC potential, one can parametrically modulate the ion-nanoparticle distance and thus the Coulomb coupling to enable a resonant interaction. For realistic parameters, we calculate that this enables sympathetic cooling of the nanoparticle to its motional ground state by a single, continuously laser-cooled ion. Additional AC drives enable the preparation of squeezed nanoparticle states and of ion-nanoparticle entanglement. Moreover, non-Gaussian states such as Fock and cat states, prepared in the ion with standard trapped-ion techniques, can be transferred to the nanoparticle with high fidelities. We provide complete protocols for each of these states, including all known decoherence sources. Our results establish electrically trapped ion-nanoparticle systems as a platform for quantum control of levitated matter.

title: Quadratic unconstrained binary optimization benchmark problems from mixed Hamming packings
comment: 36 pages, 4 figures, 'Online resource 1' included at the end of the paper
summary: Benchmarking exact solvers and noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices for quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) requires small yet challenging instances, preferably coming from actual applications. We propose such a benchmark set derived from mixed Hamming packing, a hard problem in coding theory. Starting from its mixed-integer linear programming formulation, we provide a generator for the equivalent QUBO models and study 133 instances whose optima are certified by that formulation. In the feature space of the MQLib library, we position a broad range of existing quantum-oriented benchmarks relative to the classical ones: they lie along a narrow, sparse border of the region covered by MQLib, whereas our instances form a coherent family in a region that both collections leave almost empty. Classical heuristics and a simulated bifurcation machine find the optimum of most instances quickly, in several cases sooner than an exact mixed-integer solver first encounters it, suggesting heuristic warm starts for exact solvers; for an exact QUBO solver, in turn, it appears challenging to prove optimality. In Ising form, the instances are densely connected antiferromagnets whose large local fields are almost exactly balanced by the couplings, so that the decision on each variable rests on a small remainder. This makes them hard to embed and to represent accurately on current quantum annealers, in line with our D-Wave experiments.

title: Ancilla-Free Exact Dicke-State Synthesis with Optimal Size and Depth
summary: We construct exact circuits for $n$-qubit Dicke states of any Hamming weight $k$ using $O(n)$ single-qubit gates and CNOTs in $O(\log n)$ depth without ancillary qubits. The gate count and depth are asymptotically optimal for every $0<k<n$. We compress symmetric blocks to free output qubits for weight-dependent phases. A sign correction followed by a collective rotation produces a state whose overlap with the target is at least a positive constant, so exact amplitude amplification takes $O(1)$ steps. For balanced Dicke states ($k=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$), the logarithmic depth disproves the $Ω(k)$ depth lower bound conjectured by Yuan and Zhang (2025).

title: Full-chip constrained quantum annealing via self-calibrating spin-susceptibility control
summary: Discrete optimization in finance, power grids, and logistics requires minimizing Ising Hamiltonians under coupled linear constraints. However, quadratic-penalty formulations generate dense cliques that exhaust the minor-embedding capacity of sparse superconducting processors at 128-176 spins, and first-order dual subgradient schemes diverge or stall under constraint coupling. Accordingly, this study proposes a closed-loop primal-dual scheme, designated as Self-Calibrating Quantum Susceptibility Quasi-Newton (SelfCal-QSQN), in which linear constraints are encoded in longitudinal fields and dual curvature is reconstructed from single-shot spin-fluctuation covariances. This scheme requires no penalty couplers, slack qubits, or perturbation queries. Evaluated over 891 runs on D-Wave Advantage (5,612 qubits) and Advantage2 (4,560 qubits), SelfCal-QSQN achieves 83.3% full-chip exact feasibility, reduces high-constraint error by 6.1-20.1-fold over $K$-scaled first-order updates (138.4-323.3-fold over fixed-gain curvature), outperforms time-matched mixed-integer programming at 256 spins, and attains 95.0%-96.7% feasibility on non-native and inequality benchmarks. Moreover, the scheme is robust toward shot noise and freeze-out drift.

title: Single-realization Pauli twirling for suppressing coherent error accumulation in structured quantum circuits
summary: Pauli twirling is conventionally understood as an ensemble-level noise-tailoring procedure which suppresses coherent components of the error channel by averaging over randomized compilations. This picture does not by itself determine whether a single realization of Pauli-dressed circuit can outperform its bare counterpart, nor does it predict when such an advantage should occur. In this work, we present single-realization based framework for the standard Pauli dressing of two-qubit Clifford gates in structured quantum circuits. This is afforded by the key insight that for weak coherent errors, the leading gate infidelity is governed by the variance of some accumulated error generator. Through both simulations and theoretical considerations, we verify that coherent errors accumulated at different entangling gates can produce $Θ(L^2)$ variance growth in a bare circuit, whereas independent Pauli dressing eliminates the cross-layer contribution on average and yields an $O(L)$ variance bound at any fixed confidence level for a single randomly sampled realization. We then develop a covariance diagnostic that predicts when this mechanism is effective in error mitigation. We find a strong Pauli twirling advantage for coherent errors whose transported generators have large off-diagonal covariance, and little advantage when the covariance matrix is nearly diagonal. Hardware experiments on IBM superconducting processors demonstrate fidelity improvements for GHZ-state preparation and reduced observable errors in Trotterized transverse-field Ising dynamics. These results indicate that single realizations of Pauli twirling without ensemble averaging is a useful coherent-error suppression technique for structured circuits containing repeated nontrivial two-qubit operations.

title: Beyond the Stabilizer Norm: Physicality and Resource Allocation in Pauli-Limited Quantum Certification
summary: Certification from restricted and uncertain Pauli measurements can be posed as a robust optimization problem: among all physical channels consistent with the data, how small can the fidelity with a target channel be? We first study a linear relaxation that ignores positivity and show that it is exactly characterized by a single scalar, the stabilizer norm of the target Choi state, $s_{\mathrm{wit}}(U)=\|C_U\|_{\mathrm{st}}-1/D$. We then ask whether this scalar continues to determine robustness once the positivity constraint is restored. It does not. We derive a necessary and sufficient KKT condition for the relaxation to remain tight, together with a dual obstruction certifying a strict gap, and give a rigorous computer-assisted proof that two distinct two-qubit targets can have exactly the same stabilizer norm but different physical robustness. The KKT condition depends on structure discarded by the stabilizer norm, including the support and relative signs of the Choi-Pauli coefficients and the algebraic relations among the corresponding Pauli operators. We use this structure to derive simpler sufficient certificates for a strict gap. The dual coefficients also determine how measurement uncertainty enters the finite-data fidelity bound. For a fixed budget, we derive exact shot-allocation rules for a fixed certificate and for compatible observables obtained from shared measurement settings, and we formulate the corresponding joint certificate-design problem. The conjecture that every full-support two-qubit target has positive gain remains open.

title: Penalty-Free Constrained Optimization on Dynamic Quantum Circuits via Phase-Protected Tunneling and Closed-Loop Spectral Ratchets
summary: Embedding hard operational constraints into an unconstrained Hamiltonian via large penalty multipliers induces quadratic spectral aliasing during phase estimation and increases two-qubit gate depth. This paper proposes a penalty-free, closed-loop dynamic quantum circuit scheme, designated as Zeno-decoupled gauge-ratchet optimization (Z-GRO), for constrained binary optimization without outer-loop training. Reversible feasibility phase operators within symmetric dynamical-decoupling echoes confine evolution to the feasible subspace, while an interaction-correlated commutator gauge operator resolves initial symmetry stall. Directional cooling couples the unpenalized objective Hamiltonian to a reusable ancilla with a zero-two-qubit-gate threshold offset, bypassing echoed tunneling gates on retained branches. A survival-filtered Ramsey controller advances the threshold from a linear-programming bound with automatic overshoot rollback. Exact density-matrix and trajectory simulations on spin-glass and quadratic knapsack ensembles show a single-check discrimination gain above four orders of magnitude, improving ground-state probability by factors of 3.0 to 4.3 over quantum Zeno dynamics and 11.4 to 22.5 over penalized schemes. Z-GRO reduces the spin-glass time-to-solution scaling base to 1.529 (compared to 1.684 for quantum Zeno dynamics and 1.909 to 2.047 for penalized schemes) and lowers 14-qubit knapsack time-to-solution by factors of 2.4 to 14.5. For two-qubit gate error rates between $5 \times 10^{-4}$ and $5 \times 10^{-3}$, Z-GRO achieves 2.9 to 7.0 times the optimal probability of noisy penalized feedback, while majority shielding limits loss to 6.3% at a 5.0% readout bit-flip rate, recording 0/24, 0/25, 0/96, 3/25, and 2/80 overshoots.

title: World Models for Learning Quantum Many-Body Dynamics
summary: We propose using world models for learning Hamiltonians from measured dynamics of a quantum computer or simulator. Implicitly, the parameters of a Hamiltonian are encoded in how the measured few-body observables evolve. By using a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) to perform prediction in latent space, we show that the device Hamiltonian can be efficiently inferred from noisy measurements. We train a spatiotemporal encoder and predictor with approximately $2.7$ million trainable weights using a single objective, to predict the representation of the next window of measurements from the previous one. The network is thereby driven to retain the reproducible dynamics and discard shot noise. We recover the field and coupling maps of a two-dimensional Ising lattice in real and imaginary time, and the disorder map of a one-dimensional Heisenberg chain of $100$ sites. In every settings the encoder achieves lower error than a masked autoencoder and than the same encoder left untrained. It also outperforms the same regression head applied directly to time-averaged observables, by factors of $4.4$ to $30$. We establish latent prediction as a practical self-supervised objective for learning from measurements of quantum dynamics.

title: Transpilation-Aware Multi-Vendor QPU Scheduling with Predicted Post-Transpilation Fidelity
comment: 24 pages, 11 figures, 10 tables. Code, data and scripts to reproduce all experiments: https://github.com/anapaulaappel/QPUScheduler
summary: Cluster schedulers already choose nodes, GPUs and accelerators for submitted workloads, enforce quotas and spread load. QPUs from several vendors are now schedulable resources in the same clusters, yet the user still names the device, usually the one with the best average fidelity. For a given circuit that choice is often wrong: compiling onto each device's qubit connectivity adds gates, so a job can meet its required success probability on one device and miss it on another with similar error rates, and checking this exactly by compiling for every candidate is too slow for a scheduling decision. We let the scheduler choose the QPU in two stages. A training-free estimate predicts, in milliseconds and without compiling, the success probability on every candidate and filters out those that would miss the requirement; only the chosen device then compiles the circuit, re-checks it, and binds the job or rolls back. The estimate matches compiling every candidate at about 25x lower latency in simulation, ranks measured success on IBM hardware as well as the post-compilation estimate (Spearman rho = 0.95), reduces requirement violations from tens of jobs to a few, and avoids them under contention without piling jobs onto one device. Across vendors it works when error rates are comparable (IBM and IQM) and fails when published figures overstate a device.

title: A Microwave-Photonics Formulation of the Rydberg-Atom Receiver
summary: The performance of Rydberg-atom receivers is seldom stated as a radio-frequency (RF) link budget. The receiver is shown to be an intensity-modulated direct-detection analog optical link whose modulator is the laser-driven vapor. The transmission of a warm vapor is derived in closed form by averaging the four-level response over atomic velocities. The conversion gain, noise figure, bandwidth, intercept points, and spurious-free dynamic range follow from this one function. For a weak probe the instantaneous bandwidth is half the width of the transparency window in two-photon detuning. The local-oscillator beat places the second-order intercept near twice the local-oscillator field, so the local oscillator sets the even-order linearity. For a rubidium transition at 17.04 GHz the closed forms agree with a velocity-resolved density-matrix model to 1% for the slope and the intercepts and to 10% for the bandwidth. They underestimate the group delay by a third. The response is tied to atomic constants, and the sensing volume escapes the Chu limit. However, the noise figure of a warm vapor rules it out as a general replacement for an antenna and low-noise amplifier.

title: Nonperturbative Bounds on the Ground-State Energy of Lattice QED
summary: We establish nonperturbative bounds on the ground-state energy of lattice quantum electrodynamics with naive fermions in Coulomb gauge, within the Gaussian photon approximation. Our central result is a spectral comparison theorem showing that, in the thermodynamic limit, the minimum fermionic energy density over all link configurations coincides with that of the trivial gauge configuration. The proof exploits a logarithmic determinant representation and dimensional reduction, without relying on reflection positivity, and applies to lattices of either parity. Combining this result with the positivity of the electromagnetic and Coulomb Hamiltonians, we derive an explicit lower bound on the interacting ground-state energy. Finite-lattice counterexamples show that the thermodynamic limit is essential.
